title: Slab-built butter dish with lid
subtitle: A fitted two-part dish for a standard block of butter, no kiln required
excerpt: A butter dish is two slab pieces , a shallow base and a bell-shaped lid , fitted together at leather-hard stage. This version uses air-dry clay and a drape-mould technique for the lid curve. Once sealed it keeps butter firm at room temperature for short periods, decorative use only for food contact.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Slab-building methods referenced from Encyclopedia Britannica 11th edition (1911) pottery entry. V&A open-access collection for historical ceramic form reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to an even thickness, used as the building unit in slab construction
The stage at which clay holds its shape firmly but remains damp enough to join and refine
Fully air-dried and unfired; fragile, ready for surface sealing

content.text: A butter dish is two slab pieces: a rectangular base that holds the block and a dome lid that covers it. This version works in air-dry clay with no kiln. The base is a flat
slab
with raised walls; the lid is a second slab draped over a curved support to set its arch. The finished piece is decorative and suitable for short-term covered storage.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body, thinned with water)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (for sealing)

content.text: A standard UK butter block measures roughly 13 cm x 5 cm x 5 cm. Measure yours before cutting clay. The base interior needs 2 cm of clearance on each long side and 1 cm on each short side. Roll clay on a canvas sheet or non-stick board to prevent sticking.
Making the base
Roll a slab 6 mm thick. Cut a rectangle 17 cm x 9 cm for the base floor. Lay it flat on your canvas. Cut four wall strips: two at 17 cm x 4 cm (long sides) and two at 9 cm x 4 cm (short sides).
Allow the base floor and wall strips to stiffen on the canvas for 30 minutes. They need to hold their shape before joining but must not dry past the point where slip bonds well.

Score the bottom edges of the wall strips and the perimeter of the base floor with a needle tool , a cross-hatch of shallow lines 2-3 mm apart across both surfaces. Apply slip to both scored faces. Press a long wall strip upright along one long edge of the base floor, holding firm for 20 seconds. Blend the interior join with a damp sponge.
Attach the opposite long wall, then the two short walls, in the same order. Clean each interior corner with a wooden rib, pressing clay into the joint to fill any gap.

Stand the base upright on a flat board. Press the walls gently to check they are vertical. Leave uncovered for one hour to firm to a firm-but-not-dry state. Cover loosely if the room is warm to slow drying.
Making the lid
Roll a second slab 6 mm thick. Cut a rectangle 19 cm x 11 cm. This is 1 cm wider on each side than the base exterior, which allows the lid to sit over the base walls.

Lay the slab over a drape mould , an upturned bowl or dome with a gentle curve, about 20-25 cm across at the rim. The centre of the slab rests on the dome; the edges hang down. Allow to stiffen for two to three hours until the slab holds the arch when lifted.
Roll four strips 6 mm thick for the lid walls: two at 13 cm x 2 cm and two at 7 cm x 2 cm.
Score and slip
these to the underside of the arched lid, flush with the interior edge, to form a short skirt that locates the lid over the base walls.
Press a small clay button (rolled from a walnut-sized piece of clay) to the top centre of the lid with slip for a handle. Flatten and smooth the base of the button so it bonds securely.
Fitting and drying
When both pieces have reached a firm
leather-hard

state, test the lid fit. The lid skirt should sit just inside the base walls with 1-2 mm of clearance on each side. If the fit is too tight, carefully trim the inside of the lid skirt with a fettling knife at leather-hard. Leave both pieces to air-dry separately. Do not dry them nested: they will stick or crack as the clay shrinks unevenly.
Dry both pieces
bone-dry
before sealing. This typically takes two to four days at room temperature covered loosely with a cloth. A fully dry piece is pale, lightweight, and no longer cold to the touch.
Sealing

Air-dry clay is porous. Apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water to all surfaces, allowing each coat to dry fully between applications. The seal makes the surface wipe-clean. Air-dry clay is not waterproof and is not suitable for holding liquid or for repeated washing.
Use and care

This dish is decorative. It is not food-safe without a tested glaze. Use it as a counter display, wipe with a damp cloth if needed, and avoid prolonged moisture contact. Unwrapped butter can rest in it, but wash the butter rather than the dish.
Variations
Surface-decorate the lid before drying: press a lace strip into the soft slab for texture, or use a pottery stamp for a repeating border.
Scale up by 150% for a French butter crock shape , a taller straight-sided base and a bell lid that seats inside rather than over the rim.
Score-and-slip a small clay sprig motif to the lid top in place of the button handle.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Lid does not fit , too tight
items.cause: The lid skirt was cut to match the base exterior rather than the base interior, or the clay shrank more than expected
items.fix: Trim the inside face of the lid skirt at leather-hard with a fettling knife. Work in thin passes and test the fit frequently

items.problem: Wall joint cracked at the join line
items.cause: The clay was too dry when joined (score-and-slip stopped bonding), or the join was not pressed firmly
items.fix: At leather-hard, dampen the crack, score both edges, apply fresh slip, and press closed. Support from the outside with a clay coil while the repair firms

items.cause: The slab was removed from the drape mould before it was stiff enough to hold the curve unaided
items.fix: Keep the lid on the mould until it holds its shape when tilted 45 degrees. If it has already flattened, it cannot be rearched once bone-dry

items.cause: The base was dried flat on a non-absorbent surface, causing the underside to dry slower than the top
items.fix: Dry on a plaster bat or a wooden board that can absorb some moisture. If warping starts, press the base between two flat boards under light weight overnight at leather-hard
